blocks.text: The ancient Hebrews placed honey among the things most necessary for life. Thus Sirach XXXIX, 31. Ἀρχὴ πάσης χρείας εἰς ζωὴν ἀνθρώπου, ὕδωρ, πῦρ, καὶ σίδηρος, καὶ ἅλας, καὶ σεμίδαλις πυροῦ, καὶ μέλι, etc. [Archē pasēs chreias eis zōēn anthrōpou, hydōr, pyr, kai sidēros, kai halas, kai semidalis pyrou, kai meli] The principal things of every necessity for the life of man (that is, they hold first place among the things most required for life) are water, fire, iron, salt, grain, fine flour, honey, etc. For honey was useful for many purposes: for food, for drink, for medicine, for [col. 525] preserving corpses. Finally, superstitious people used honey in their rites. As for the eating of honey, Jonathan in his Paraphrase on Lev. XI, 20 says of it: The kinds [III, 388] of bees shall be an abomination to you. Yet דובשא דזיבורי יתאכל, the honey of bees shall be eaten. The Arabs write the same thing, and illustrate it by the example of human milk, the drinking of which is permitted, although human flesh is forbidden. Accordingly the eating of honey is dealt with here and there in Scripture. Thus Deuter. XXXII, 13. He gave him honey to suck from the rock. Psal. LXXXI, 17. With honey from the rock I will satisfy you. Prov. XXIV, 13. My son, eat honey, because it is good. Prov. XXV, 16. When you find honey, eat as much as is sufficient for you. Esa. VII, 22. Whoever is left in the land shall eat butter and honey. Ezech. XVI, 13. You ate fine flour and honey and oil. Examples are Samson, Iudic. XIV, 9; Jonathan, 1 Sam. XIV, 27; Solomon, Cant. V, 1; John, Matth. III, 4; and finally Christ himself, Luc. XXIV, 42. 43. That this food also suits infancy is proved from the celebrated passage of Isaiah about Emmanuel, ch. VII, 15: He shall eat butter and honey, until he knows to refuse evil and choose good: that is, until he is a little older. Basil: Παιδικῇ τροφῇ χρῆται ὁ Ἐμμανουὴλ διὰ τὴν σάρκα, βουτύρῳ, καὶ μέλιτι· [Paidikē trophē chrētai ho Emmanouēl dia tēn sarka, boutyrō, kai meliti] Because of the flesh Emmanuel uses a child's food, namely butter and honey. Cyril: Τροφὴν αὐτῷ γεγεννῆσθαι λέγων τὴν νηπίοις πρέπουσαν, βούτηρόν τε, καὶ μέλι· [Trophēn autō gegennēsthai legōn tēn nēpiois prepousan, boutēron te, kai meli] Saying that his food would be what suits little children, butter and honey. Jerome: He uses the foods of infancy, „He shall eat butter and honey.“ Bernard, On Advent, Sermon 2: „He shall eat butter, he says, and milk: as if he were saying, He will be a little child, and will feed on infant foods.“ Hence the ancients gave milk and honey to be tasted beforehand at baptism, in which the faithful are reborn. Tertullian, De corona militis ch. 3: Then, having been taken up, we first taste the concord of milk and honey. Alluding to this, Jerome, against the Luciferians, chapter 4, says that those who have come out of the font first taste the concord of milk and honey as a sign of infancy. For infants were then fed not on milk alone but also on honey. Thus Didymus relates from the most ancient histories of the Cretans that Melisseus, king of the Cretans, had two daughters, Amalthea and Melissa, who nourished the boy Jupiter with goat's milk and honey. So it is found in Lactantius, book 1, On False Religion, ch. 22. And in Antoninus Liberalis, Boeus mentions a cave occupied by ἱεραὶ μέλιτται τροφοὶ τοῦ Διὸς [hierai melittai trophoi tou Dios], sacred bees, nurses of Jupiter. Of the same kind is the story that Πινδάρῳ, τῆς πατρῴας οἰκίας ἐκτεθέντι, μέλιτται τροφοὶ ἐγένοντο ὑπὲρ τοῦ γάλακτος παρατεθεῖσαι μέλι [Pindarō, tēs patrōas oikias ektethenti, melittai trophoi egenonto hyper tou galaktos paratetheisai meli]: for Pindar, driven from his father's house and exposed, bees took the place of nurses, offering him honey instead of milk. Accordingly, if children who were ill had to drink something bitter, the rim of the cup was first smeared with honey, so that they would think their usual food was being offered them. Lucretius:

But as physicians, when they try to give children loathsome wormwood, first touch the rims around the cups with the sweet golden liquid of honey, so that the unsuspecting age of children may be deceived. [III, 389] But although honey is a pleasant food and suits any age, one must nevertheless take care not to overdo it. Hence Solomon, Proverb. XXV, 16: When you find honey, eat as much as is enough for you, lest being sated you vomit it up. And Prov. XXVII, 7: The sated soul tramples on the honeycomb. As Pindar, Nemean 7:
Κόρον δ᾽ ἔχει, καὶ μέλι. [Koron d' echei, kai meli.]
Even of honey there is satiety. And an old Epigram:
— — καὶ μέλιτος τὸ πλέον ἐστὶ χόλη, [kai melitos to pleon esti cholē]
Even of honey, what is in excess is gall. A rabbinic proverb also belongs here: אוכל דבש הרבה סופו מקיאה, He who eats much honey vomits it up in the end.
